title: Planning for transition from day one
blurb: Explain what a successful transition needs, why business as usual must be considered throughout, and why transition is planned from the outset.
question: A food distributor plans to switch on a new warehouse management system in November, its busiest month. Staff training is pencilled in for 'after go-live' and the IT helpdesk hasn't been told. What basic requirements for a successful transition are being missed?

teach.h: From 'the project' to 'how we work now'
teach.body: Transition is the integration of the project's outputs into business as usual (BAU), so that the benefits can be realised. In plain English, it is the hand-off from the temporary project to the permanent organisation that will run, support and use what was built. APM's basic requirements are to consider BAU THROUGHOUT the project and to plan for transition FROM THE OUTSET, not as an afterthought once the outputs are finished.

left.label: Project
items: Temporary
Creates change
Led by the PM

right.label: Business as usual
items: Ongoing
Absorbs change
Led by ops managers

both.label: TRANSITION
items: Users
Readiness
Handover
Support period

teach.caption: Transition is the overlap: the project can't succeed without BAU, and BAU can't benefit unless the project hands over well.

steps.label: Concept
steps.sub: Involve operations; identify BAU impacts and constraints

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: Transition approach in the PMP; acceptance and readiness criteria

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Users test and train; avoid BAU peak periods

teach.caption: Transition is the last linear phase, but its planning starts in the first.

head: Area
Ready means…
rows: Right staff in place, roles agreed, change accepted
New ways of working written and agreed
Live, integrated, with access set up
Users and support staff trained in time
Manuals, guides and records handed over
teach.caption: Plus agreed acceptance criteria, a handover plan with timing, and a support period after go-live.

teach.h: Why plan transition from the outset
teach.body: Choices made early decide how easy the outputs are to run: a design that needs twice the staff, or a go-live in the busiest month, is cheap to fix on paper and costly to fix later. BAU has its own calendar (peak periods, system freezes, maintenance windows, staff availability) that the schedule must respect. Training, support and readiness need budget and time. Leave it late and the outputs arrive to a business that can't use them, so benefits are delayed or lost.

teach.h: Transition activities run through the schedule
teach.caption: Engagement with BAU spans almost the whole project. Training finishes BEFORE go-live, and support continues after it.

rows.label: BAU involvement
values: Planned at key points and gates
Continuous, via the product owner and users

rows.label: Risk
values: Spread, but BAU must be ready repeatedly

teach.body: Hartley's operations manager joined the project in Concept and flagged November as peak season, so go-live moved to late January. She helped design pick routes, which avoided an extra shift. Super-users were trained a month before go-live and coached colleagues. The IT service desk received scripts and a support contract, and a six-week support period with the supplier on site was agreed. Benefits tracking started the week after go-live.

teach.text: The classic distractors: 'plan the handover once the outputs are built', 'involve operations at acceptance testing', 'train users after go-live'. All are wrong. The requirement is to consider BAU THROUGHOUT and plan transition FROM THE OUTSET. Transition is not the same as closure either: closure ends the project, transition embeds its outputs.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define transition: integrating outputs into BAU so benefits can be realised.
Explain considering BAU throughout: involve users and operations from Concept onwards.
Explain planning from the outset: design for operability, respect BAU peaks, budget for training and support.
List business readiness: people, processes, systems, training, support and documentation.
State the consequence of late planning: outputs the business can't use, so benefits are delayed or lost.
Transition: integrating the project's outputs into BAU so benefits can be realised.
Consider BAU throughout the project and plan transition from the outset.
Business readiness: people, processes, systems, training, support, documentation.
Also needed: acceptance criteria, a handover plan and timing, and a support period.
Linear: one main transition at the end. Iterative: a transition with every release.

summary: You can now explain what transition is and list the basic requirements for a successful one. You can also explain why BAU must be considered throughout the project and why transition is planned from the outset in both linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: What is the main purpose of transition in a project?
options: To integrate the outputs into business as usual
To close the project's contracts and its accounts
To move the project manager onto a new project
To agree the business case with the sponsor
A.why: Transition integrates the project's outputs into BAU so that the benefits can be realised.

whyNot.1: Closing contracts and accounts is part of project closure, not the purpose of transition.
whyNot.2: Reassigning the PM happens at closure and isn't the aim of transition.
whyNot.3: The business case is agreed in Concept and Definition.

A.q: When should planning for transition begin?
options: Once deployment is complete
At the final decision gate
After the post-project review
At the outset of the project
A.why: APM's requirement is to plan for transition from the outset, so design, schedule and budget all allow for it.

whyNot.0: By then it's too late to design for operability or fit around BAU.
whyNot.1: The final gate confirms readiness; planning must start much earlier.
whyNot.2: The post-project review comes after transition.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT part of business readiness for transition?
options: Staff trained in the new processes
Support desk ready before go-live
The project team's next assignment
Updated user guides and manuals
A.why: Business readiness is about BAU being able to run and support the outputs. The project team's next role is a resourcing matter, not readiness.

whyNot.0: Trained staff are a core part of readiness.
whyNot.1: Support arrangements must be in place for go-live.
whyNot.3: Users need up-to-date documentation to work in the new way.

B.q: A retailer plans to replace its tills during the Christmas peak. The operations team warns this is their busiest period. What does this illustrate?
options: A success factor for the till supplier
A dependency between project and BAU
A KPI for the project's delivery team
An acceptance criterion for the tills
B.why: BAU peak periods constrain when change can be absorbed, which is a dependency the project schedule must respect.

whyNot.0: A success factor is a condition that helps success, not a BAU constraint.
whyNot.2: A KPI measures progress; this is a scheduling constraint.
whyNot.3: Acceptance criteria define what the tills must do, not when they can go in.

B.q: Why should operational users be involved throughout the project rather than only at handover?
options: So the PM can leave the project early
So the budget is released more quickly
So outputs fit how BAU really works
So fewer acceptance tests are needed
B.why: Involving BAU throughout means outputs are designed for how the business actually operates, and people are ready to use them.

whyNot.0: User involvement doesn't shorten the PM's role.
whyNot.1: Budget release is governed by gates, not user involvement.
whyNot.3: Acceptance testing is still required; involvement makes it smoother.

B.q: In an iterative life cycle, how does transition typically differ from a linear one?
options: It isn't needed, as users test every time box
It is led by the supplier, not by the business
It takes place before the Foundations phase
It happens at each release, not only at the end
B.why: Iterative Deployment repeats, so increments transition into BAU release by release, and BAU must be ready each time.

whyNot.0: Testing in time boxes doesn't remove the need to embed outputs in BAU.
whyNot.1: The business, through the sponsor and users, leads adoption in either model.
whyNot.2: Foundations comes before any outputs exist to transition.

C.q: A local authority's new waste-collection app goes live. Crews were never trained, the helpdesk has no scripts and complaints soar. Which requirement was MOST clearly missed?
options: Supplier selection
Business readiness
Benefits identification
Configuration control
C.why: Untrained crews and an unprepared helpdesk mean the business wasn't ready to operate and support the outputs.

whyNot.0: Supplier choice isn't the problem; the business wasn't prepared.
whyNot.2: The benefits may be well identified; the failure was readiness.
whyNot.3: Configuration control manages versions of items, not BAU preparation.

C.q: A design choice will double the staff needed to run a new system. When is the best time for this to be spotted?
options: Early, by involving BAU in design
At handover, during acceptance
After go-live, in the support period
At the final post-project review
C.why: Considering BAU throughout, starting early in design, catches operability problems while they are still cheap to change.

whyNot.1: At handover the design is built; changing it is costly.
whyNot.2: After go-live the extra cost is already locked in.
whyNot.3: A post-project review records the lesson but is too late for this project.

C.q: What is the main purpose of an agreed support period after go-live?
options: To let the team add features users missed
To delay formal acceptance of the outputs
To keep the project budget open for good
To help BAU settle and fix early problems
C.why: A support period gives BAU help while it beds in the new outputs and resolves early problems, before full ownership.

whyNot.0: New features go through change control or the backlog, not the support period.
whyNot.1: Acceptance criteria are agreed in advance; support isn't a way to delay acceptance.
whyNot.2: The support period is time-limited and the project still closes.

reteach.title: Opening a new restaurant
reteach.question: A restaurant owner builds a beautiful new kitchen, then realises on opening night that the chefs haven't practised the menu and no suppliers are booked. What should she have planned from day one?

blocks.h: The kitchen is not the restaurant
blocks.body: The fit-out is the project; running the restaurant every night is business as usual. A smart owner involves the head chef while the kitchen is designed (so it suits how they cook), avoids opening in the week of a big local festival, books suppliers, trains staff with practice nights before opening, and keeps the fitter on call for the first few weeks. None of that can be bolted on at the end.

blocks.h: Opening night, planned from day one

blocks.text: A finished kitchen with untrained staff is like delivered outputs with an unready business: everything is built, and nothing is gained.

explain.body: Transition integrates the project's outputs into business as usual. It matters because outputs only create value once BAU is using them.

test.q: Why does transition matter so much for benefits?
options: It is when the benefits are first identified
It fixes the project budget for good
Outputs only create value once used in BAU
It replaces the need for benefit owners
test.why: Benefits come from outcomes, which require outputs to be adopted and used in BAU.

whyNot.3: Benefit owners are still needed after transition.

explain.body: Involve users and operations managers from Concept onwards: in requirements, design reviews, testing and planning. They know how the business really works and what it can absorb.

test.q: Which action BEST shows BAU being considered throughout a project?
options: Ops managers join design reviews from day one
Ops are emailed the go-live date in week one
The PM writes the user manual alone at the end
Training is arranged after go-live complaints
test.why: Active involvement of operations in design from the start is what considering BAU throughout looks like.

whyNot.1: Telling people a date is informing, not involving.
whyNot.2: Writing guides alone and late ignores BAU's knowledge.
whyNot.3: Reactive training after complaints is the opposite of planning for BAU.

explain.body: The transition approach belongs in the project management plan from Definition, with time and budget for training, readiness and support, and a schedule that respects BAU peaks and freezes.

test.q: What is the MAIN risk of leaving transition planning until deployment ends?
options: The business case will lack costs
Success criteria will be met too early
The critical path will have no tasks
The business won't be ready to use it
test.why: Without early planning, training, support and process changes aren't ready, so outputs arrive to a business that can't use them.

whyNot.0: Costs are in the business case from the start.
whyNot.1: Late planning tends to cause shortfalls, not early success.
whyNot.2: The critical path exists regardless of transition planning.

explain.body: Before go-live, check people, processes, systems, training, support and documentation are ready, along with acceptance criteria, the handover plan and the support period.

test.q:
Which TWO are business readiness checks?
1) Staff have been trained
2) Final supplier invoices are paid
3) Support arrangements are in place
4) Team members are reassigned
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
test.why: Trained staff and support arrangements show BAU can operate and support the outputs.

whyNot.0: Paying invoices is financial close-down, not readiness.
whyNot.2: Invoices and reassignment are closure activities.
whyNot.3: Support is readiness, but reassigning the team is a closure activity.
